scope: Score a transcript excerpt from a HIMR recording as one unit, evaluating the overall language and content across all voices represented. Do not assign enduring traits to Daniel or any named person. Passages may be edited, performed, quoted, transcribed inaccurately, or spoken by someone else. Use only the supplied excerpt and its transcript metadata. The question bank is exploratory and has not been psychometrically validated.
instructions: Answer each question independently using only this excerpt. Do not infer missing context or use a speaker name as evidence.

For score items, use the five item-specific ordered descriptions. If the excerpt is too short, unintelligible, or lacks enough relevant evidence to rate the requested dimension, abstain rather than treating missing evidence as zero. A clear, intelligible excerpt that simply does not express the item may receive 0.

Scores describe observable language or a hypothetical viewer response, not the speaker's inner feelings, stable personality, honesty, diagnosis, identity, or the truth of an allegation. Attribute quoted emotions or actions to the person the text names, not automatically to the current speaker.
Controversial claims may be rated for discourse style, rhetoric, and anticipated reception. Do not decide whether claims are true.

For categories, choose unknown or not inferable when evidence is insufficient. Textual cues to multiple speakers or synthetic speech are not proof about the audio. Do not infer text-to-speech from unusual wording alone.

score_scale.note: Each score item supplies its own complete ordered anchors. Use those anchors rather than assuming every item has the same direction. For evidence-intensity items, 0 means no evidence in an intelligible applicable excerpt; abstention means insufficient evidence to rate.

questions.instructions: Is this excerpt intelligible and long enough to assess its verbal presentation? Judge rating feasibility only, not whether any particular style trait is present.

criteria.true: Yes: enough intelligible language is present to rate verbal presentation.
criteria.false: No: too little or too unclear to rate verbal presentation.

questions.instructions: Is this excerpt intelligible and long enough to assess emotion conveyed by its language? Judge rating feasibility only, not whether emotion is expressed.

criteria.true: Yes: enough intelligible language is present to rate conveyed affect.
criteria.false: No: too little or too unclear to rate conveyed affect.

questions.instructions: Is there enough intelligible content to estimate a hypothetical viewer's immediate response to this excerpt? Do not judge whether a real audience saw or liked it.

criteria.true: Yes: enough intelligible content is present for a cautious hypothetical response estimate.
criteria.false: No: too little or too unclear to estimate a hypothetical response.

questions.instructions: Does the excerpt contain clearly quoted, reenacted, or reported speech whose viewpoint should be distinguished from the excerpt's overall narration?

criteria.true: Yes: a distinct quoted, reenacted, or reported voice is evident.
criteria.false: No such distinct voice is evident in the excerpt.

questions.instructions: Does the supplied transcript itself mark this excerpt as unintelligible, uncertain, or otherwise transcription-ambiguous? Do not infer uncertainty merely because wording is informal.

criteria.true: Yes: explicit uncertainty or unintelligibility is marked in the supplied transcript.
criteria.false: No such uncertainty is marked in the supplied transcript.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker's own language give an impression of sociability or social engagement?
criteria: A slight cue of social engagement.
A moderate cue of social engagement.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker state views or direct the conversation with assertiveness?
How strongly does the wording itself convey verbal energy or animation? Do not use audio volume or pitch.
How strongly does the speaker's own wording convey compassion or concern for others?
How strongly does the speaker's own wording convey respect toward people discussed?
How strongly does the speaker's own wording convey willingness to give others the benefit of the doubt?
How strongly is the speaker's explanation organized and easy to follow?
criteria: Slight organization; mostly difficult to follow.
Moderate organization with some clear links.
Strongly organized and generally easy to follow.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker persist in explaining or supporting a point?
criteria: Moderate effort to continue or support a point.
Strong, repeated effort to develop a point.
Very sustained effort to develop or reinforce a point.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker's own wording express responsibility for their stated actions or commitments?
criteria: Strong or repeated ownership of actions or commitments.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker's wording convey curiosity or active interest in ideas?
How strongly does the speaker acknowledge alternative views or openness to reconsidering a point?
criteria: A moderate cue, such as limited acknowledgment of alternatives.
Strong acknowledgment or consideration of alternatives.
Very sustained openness to alternatives or revision.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker use imaginative, novel, or creative framing?
criteria: A moderate creative or novel framing.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the wording convey a calm, even-handed presentation?
criteria: A moderate calm and measured presentation.
Exceptionally steady and measured wording throughout.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker's wording convey worry or apprehension? Rate expression only, not a trait or diagnosis.
How strongly does the speaker's own wording criticize or devalue themselves?
How strongly does the speaker present their own statements as certain or categorical? This rates delivery, not factual accuracy.
criteria: A moderate degree of categorical presentation.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker qualify, hedge, or signal uncertainty about their own statements?
criteria: Very pervasive qualification or uncertainty marking.

questions.instructions: How directly does the speaker state the main point rather than approaching it indirectly?
criteria: No direct statement of a point.

questions.instructions: Where does the overall emotional tone conveyed by the speaker's own language fall from negative to positive? Rate expressed tone, not underlying feeling.
How activated or emotionally energized is the tone conveyed by the language, from subdued to highly energized?
criteria: Very subdued or no activation cue.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker's own language convey amusement or playfulness?
How strongly does the speaker's own language convey joy or enthusiasm?
criteria: Strong or repeated joy or enthusiasm.
Very prominent, sustained joy or enthusiasm.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker's own language convey affection, warmth, or care?
criteria: Strong or repeated warmth or care.
Very prominent, sustained warmth or care.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker's own language convey hope or optimism?
criteria: Strong or repeated hope or optimism.
Very prominent, sustained hope or optimism.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker's own language convey interest or curiosity about its subject?
How strongly does the speaker's own language convey pride or self-satisfaction?
How strongly does the speaker's own language convey anger?
How strongly does the speaker's own language convey irritation or annoyance?
How strongly does the speaker's own language convey fear or anxiety?
criteria: Strong or repeated fear or anxiety.
Very prominent, sustained fear or anxiety.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker's own language convey sadness or grief?
How strongly does the speaker's own language convey disappointment?
How strongly does the speaker's own language convey disgust or revulsion?
How strongly does the speaker's own language convey embarrassment or shame?
criteria: Strong or repeated embarrassment or shame.
Very prominent, sustained embarrassment or shame.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker use humor or joking in their own narration?
criteria: A slight joke or humorous cue.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker use irony or sarcasm in their own narration?
criteria: No clear irony or sarcasm cue.
A moderate and reasonably clear cue.
Strong or repeated irony or sarcasm.
Irony or sarcasm is exceptionally prominent throughout.

questions.instructions: How much personal experience or personal information does the speaker disclose about themselves?
How strongly does the speaker directly address viewers or an online audience?
criteria: A moderate amount of direct address.
Direct audience address is sustained throughout.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker try to persuade the audience to accept a viewpoint or take an action?
criteria: Persuasion is sustained and central throughout.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker apologize for their own stated action or words?
criteria: An explicit, sustained apology with clear ownership.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker criticize or condemn a person, group, or action? Rate discourse, not whether the criticism is justified.
How strongly does the excerpt present disagreement, confrontation, or interpersonal conflict?
How strongly does the speaker answer or rebut an opposing claim?
criteria: Rebuttal is sustained and central throughout.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker offer concrete examples, sources, or reasons to support their own claims? Do not assess whether they are true.
criteria: No supporting reasons or examples offered.
A slight or vague support cue.

questions.instructions: How strongly is the excerpt organized as a narrative with events or a sequence over time?
criteria: A strongly developed narrative structure throughout.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker repeat or restate a point for emphasis?
How strongly does the speaker use emphatic or intensifying wording?
criteria: A moderate amount of emphatic wording.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker invite or urge viewers to do something?
criteria: No request or call to action.
A strong or repeated call to action.
A sustained and prominent call to action.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker redirect away from a question or point raised within the excerpt?
criteria: No redirection from an evident point.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker distinguish what they know from what they do not know or cannot confirm?
criteria: Knowledge boundaries are explicit and consistently maintained.

questions.instructions: How much does the speaker quote, reenact, or report another person's words? Exclude the speaker's own unquoted narration.
criteria: A moderate amount of reported speech.
Reported or reenacted speech dominates the excerpt.

questions.instructions: How strongly does the speaker use questions directed to viewers to invite a response or reflection?
criteria: Viewer-directed questions are a sustained device.

questions.instructions: How much does the speaker provide concrete scene-setting details such as place, time, or circumstances?
How strongly does the excerpt state an outcome, resolution, or next step to the events discussed?
criteria: No outcome or next step stated.
A slight or uncertain outcome cue.
A stated but limited outcome or next step.
A clear outcome or next step.
A detailed, emphatic resolution or plan.

questions.instructions: For a general adult viewer seeing only this transcript excerpt, with no prior knowledge of the creator, how likely is it to prompt interest in hearing more?
How likely is a general adult viewer to find this excerpt amusing?
criteria: Very unlikely to find it amusing.

questions.instructions: How likely is a general adult viewer to feel empathy for someone discussed in this excerpt?
How likely is this excerpt to prompt disagreement or pushback from some general adult viewers?
How likely is this excerpt to make some general adult viewers uncomfortable?
How likely is a general adult viewer to find this excerpt confusing without additional context?
How likely is this excerpt to prompt a viewer to comment or respond? Estimate conversational provocation, not measured engagement.
criteria: Very unlikely to prompt a response.

questions.instructions: How likely is a general adult viewer to share this excerpt with someone else?
How likely is a general adult viewer to find the speaker's presentation credible or trustworthy based only on this excerpt's presentation? Do not judge truth.
criteria: Very unlikely to create that impression.

questions.instructions: How likely is a general adult viewer to want to continue watching after this excerpt?
How likely is the excerpt to produce sharply differing reactions across viewers?
Choose the best single category for the excerpt's main content. Use mixed if two or more are equally central and unknown if insufficient evidence.

criteria.personal_vlog: Personal update, daily-life narration, or informal vlog.
criteria.livestream_chat: Live-stream conversation, chat response, or real-time audience interaction.
criteria.commentary_drama: Commentary or account centered on conflict, criticism, allegations, or interpersonal controversy.
criteria.storytime: Retrospective personal story or narrative of past events.
criteria.gaming: Gameplay, game commentary, or game-related discussion.
criteria.travel: Travel, place visit, or location-focused account.
criteria.relationship: Dating, romance, or relationship discussion without conflict as the main focus.
criteria.other: A clear main category not listed above.
criteria.mixed: Several listed categories are similarly central.
criteria.unknown: Insufficient evidence to choose a category.

questions.instructions: Based only on wording and transcript speaker labels in this excerpt, is more than one distinct speaking voice represented? Do not infer acoustic speakers from punctuation alone.

criteria.yes: Clear transcript evidence of two or more distinct speaking voices.
criteria.no: The excerpt reads as one speaking voice, with no clear second voice represented.
criteria.uncertain: Some evidence of another voice, but attribution is ambiguous.

questions.instructions: What evidence, if any, does the transcript text provide that speech is text-to-speech or synthetic? This is a text-only evidence classification, not a determination about the audio.

criteria.explicit: The text explicitly identifies speech as text-to-speech, synthetic, or computer-generated.
criteria.playback_possible: The text refers to playback, a recording, or an imitated voice, but does not establish text-to-speech.
criteria.no_text_evidence: No explicit text evidence about text-to-speech or synthetic speech.

questions.instructions: Which presentation mode is most evident from the text? Choose one.

criteria.reported_story: Primarily reports another person's account or events.
criteria.direct_commentary: Primarily evaluates or comments on a topic or event.
criteria.mixed: Two or more modes are similarly central.

questions.instructions: Is the excerpt explicitly addressed to viewers or an online audience?

criteria.yes: Direct viewer or audience address is explicit.
criteria.no: No direct viewer or audience address is evident.
criteria.uncertain: Possible, but not clear from the text.

questions.instructions: Does the transcript explicitly signal that another person's speech is quoted, reenacted, or played back?

criteria.playback: Explicit reference to audio/video playback or a recording.
criteria.both: Both quoted/reenacted speech and playback are signaled.

questions.instructions: How usable is the supplied text for interpretation of the excerpt? This is about text evidence only.

criteria.minor_noise: Interpretable with a few likely transcription errors.
criteria.substantial_noise: Meaning is materially obscured by transcription issues.

questions.instructions: How specific is the subject matter in this excerpt?

criteria.specific: A clearly identifiable, narrow subject or event.
criteria.broad: A broad topic without a narrow focus.
criteria.multiple: Several topics without one dominant subject.

questions.instructions: Which textual presentation style best describes the excerpt?

criteria.spontaneous: Informal, conversational wording with signs of spontaneous speech.
criteria.scripted: Text strongly suggests a prepared or read script.
criteria.performed: Clearly staged, role-played, or theatrical wording.

factor_analysis.notes: Eligibility means exploratory analysis only; it does not establish that items measure latent traits. Analyze recording- or passage-level observations with missingness and repeated-measure structure accounted for. Keep categorical classifiers separate. Examine factor stability and item behavior before naming dimensions.

references.citation: Soto & John (2017), The Next Big Five Inventory (BFI-2)
references.use: Human Big Five domain/facet framework; original transcript items here are not copied BFI-2 items or a validated personality test.

references.citation: Soto & John (2017), BFI-2 short forms
references.use: Human psychometric measure tradeoffs; informs construct domains only.

references.citation: Fleeson (2001), traits as density distributions of states
references.use: Repeated behavioral states vary within people; aggregate distributions rather than equating one excerpt with a stable trait.

references.citation: Russell (1980), a circumplex model of affect
references.use: Affect valence/activation as dimensional descriptive axes.

references.citation: Watson, Clark & Tellegen (1988), PANAS
references.use: Validated self-report positive/negative affect measure; not an observer transcript measure.

references.citation: Schwartz et al. (2013), personality and language of social media
references.use: Large Facebook sample links language patterns to self-reported traits; observational, platform-specific evidence.

references.citation: Peters & Matz (2024), LLMs infer psychological dispositions of social-media users
references.use: Tests inference from Facebook status updates; trait agreement varies and does not validate long third-party transcripts.

references.citation: Peters, Cerf & Matz (2024), LLM personality from free-form interactions
references.use: Preprint; personality-relevant elicitation produced better inference than naturalistic/default chat, a different setting from archived videos.

references.citation: Zhu, Jin & Coifman (2025), personality inference from real-world conversations
references.use: Preprint benchmark on 555 interviews reports weak criterion validity despite high repeatability.

references.citation: Sühr et al. (2025), challenging personality tests for LLMs
references.use: LLM self-test results are prompt-sensitive and may not share human factor structure; distinct task but key validity warning.

references.citation: Huang et al. (2024), reliability of psychological scales on LLMs
references.use: Repeated outputs can be consistent while validity remains a separate question.

references.citation: Gilardi, Alizadeh & Kubli (2023), ChatGPT for text annotation
references.use: LLM performance on topic, stance, relevance, and frame coding; does not establish personality or emotion measurement validity.

references.citation: Demszky et al. (2020), GoEmotions
references.use: Human-labeled fine-grained Reddit emotion corpus; reports substantial task difficulty and domain-specific limitations.

references.citation: Poria et al. (2019), MELD
references.use: Multi-party conversational affect benchmark; finds context and multimodal cues relevant beyond transcript text.

references.citation: Wood et al. (2018), comparison of emotion annotation schemes
references.use: Study on tweets found better agreement for dimensional rating scales than discrete basic-emotion labels in their comparison.

references.citation: Pavlick & Kwiatkowski (2019), inherent disagreements in textual inference
references.use: Human annotation disagreement can persist as plausible variation; retain distributions where possible.

references.citation: Plank (2022), human label variation
references.use: Methodological argument for representing legitimate label variation rather than assuming one unambiguous answer.

references.citation: Tafesse (2020), YouTube optimization and video views
references.use: Observational trending-video study; metadata associations with views do not validate transcript-only predictions.

references.citation: Cui et al. (2024), video views and sentiment in titles/thumbnails
references.use: Observational study of video cover elements; packaging is distinct from transcript content.

references.citation: Crane & Sornette (2008), YouTube popularity dynamics
references.use: Large video time-series study distinguishes endogenous diffusion and exogenous bursts; views cannot be read directly from transcript content.
